body: THE GOOD NUMBER: for years GE delivered steady, predictable earnings that met or beat guidance, a moderate P/E and a long dividend record; the stock was ~$30-32 in mid-2016. WHY IT LIED: earnings that smooth across power turbines, aviation and a finance arm are improbable; GE Capital and accounting choices absorbed volatility. Industrial cash flow was flattered by selling receivables to GE Capital and by 'deferred monetisation' (booking service-contract profits ahead of cash, so contract assets grew faster than revenue); the dividend exceeded free cash flow; a run-off long-term-care insurance book was under-reserved (Jan 2018: $6.2 bn after-tax charge plus ~$15 bn reserve top-ups); Alstom (2015) was bought at the power cycle peak ($22 bn goodwill impairment, Oct 2018). Dividend halved Nov 2017 and cut to $0.01 in 2018; stock ~$6.7 by Dec 2018. TEST: compare reported earnings volatility with what the businesses' cycles imply; dividend cover by FCF; trend of contract assets and factored receivables; ask what long-tail liabilities sit in a finance subsidiary. LESSON: unusually smooth earnings in cyclical businesses are a sign of management, not of quality.

data.good_number: decades of steady EPS beats, 'reasonable' P/E, long dividend record, AAA-era reputation
data.test_that_catches_it: dividend vs FCF; contract assets vs revenue; receivables sold; earnings volatility too low for the businesses
data.why_misleading: smoothness came from GE Capital and accounting levers (receivable factoring, contract-asset 'deferred monetisation'); hidden long-term-care insurance liability

title: Hidden trap: GE's smooth earnings, low P/E and dividend
